headline: The AI boom is still real—but markets are repricing it
dek: Across the United States, China, Japan, and South Korea, artificial intelligence is reshaping investment, exports, currencies, and economic policy. The benefits are substantial, but uneven.
story_title: AI’s next test: from explosive growth to economic broadening
story_html:
United States 🇺🇸 The clearest warning came from Wall Street. A sharp sell-off in artificial-intelligence shares pushed the S&P 500 down 3.7% on Friday, while the Nasdaq entered negative territory for the year. Chipmakers and companies linked to data-centre construction suffered especially heavy losses. Investors are not necessarily abandoning AI; rather, they are questioning whether exceptionally high valuations and enormous capital spending can be justified by near-term profits. The episode shows how quickly a powerful investment narrative can become a source of market vulnerability. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/stock-markets-anthropic-ai-chips-boom-c4c3f4878b12989347f8a930ed813dad))

China 🇨🇳 China illustrates a more complicated picture. Broad mainland equity indexes fell on November 20, and the yuan weakened modestly, but Chinese technology shares connected with domestic computing and advanced chip packaging also attracted interest. Chinese financial coverage has highlighted efforts to strengthen locally designed AI infrastructure, including packaging, processors, and supporting equipment. This suggests that Beijing’s AI strategy is partly defensive: it aims not only to capture a commercial boom, but also to reduce dependence on foreign technology. China is therefore participating in the AI cycle while simultaneously building a more self-reliant supply chain. ([chinaday.news](https://www.chinaday.news/en))

Japan 🇯🇵 Japan is feeling the same technology shock through both markets and monetary policy. The Nikkei fell sharply alongside other Asian equity indexes after the U.S. technology rout. At the same time, the Bank of Japan is moving into unfamiliar territory: inflation has reached its 2% target, yet policymakers disagree about how far interest rates should eventually rise. Reuters reports that markets broadly expect another hike in December, but uncertainty about the neutral rate is encouraging yen selling. Japan must therefore balance three pressures—higher import costs from a weak yen, stronger inflation, and the risk that tighter policy will weaken household consumption. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/analysisbojs-ambiguity-on-rate-hike-path-could-tempt-yen-bears-5040426))

South Korea 🇰🇷 Korea represents the export side of the story. It passed $1 trillion in annual exports for the first time, with high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, chips playing a central role in the surge. Yet the achievement has exposed a structural divide. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are benefiting enormously, while some smaller suppliers remain loss-making and several traditional industries face intense competition from China. The common theme, then, is not simply “AI growth.” It is the challenge of converting a concentrated technology boom into durable, broad-based prosperity. Markets, governments, and companies are now testing whether AI can move from spectacular valuation story to productive economic foundation. ([news.sbs.co.kr](https://news.sbs.co.kr/english/article.do?news_id=N1008854652))
b2_summary: The four economies are connected by the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and semiconductors. In the United States, investors have started to question very high AI valuations and heavy spending. China is developing domestic AI chips and equipment while trying to reduce reliance on foreign technology. Japan is dealing with market volatility, inflation, and uncertainty about future interest-rate increases. South Korea has reached $1 trillion in exports, helped by HBM memory chips, but smaller firms and older industries are not benefiting equally. The main question is whether AI can create broad economic growth rather than gains for only a few companies.

common_theme: The AI and semiconductor boom is creating powerful growth and export opportunities, but it is also producing market volatility, policy dilemmas, and uneven benefits across companies and economies.

concept.title: What is the neutral interest rate?
concept.explanation: The neutral rate is the approximate interest rate at which the economy grows at a normal pace without strong inflation pressure or a recessionary drag. If a central bank sets rates below it, borrowing is generally encouraged; if it sets rates above it, demand is usually restrained. The difficulty is that the neutral rate cannot be observed directly, so policymakers must estimate it.

quiz.question: Why is the Bank of Japan’s neutral rate important in today’s story?
options: It determines how much China can export.
It helps show whether future Japanese rate hikes would stimulate or restrain the economy.
It measures the number of HBM chips Korea exports.
quiz.explanation: The neutral rate is a benchmark for judging whether monetary policy is still supportive or has become restrictive.

one_sentence: The next phase of the AI boom will be judged not by how high valuations rise, but by how widely productivity gains spread.
